title: The Goddess Who Binds and Frees
hookLine: two betrayed men ask why they can't stop caring
carry: mahamaya: the goddess's power binds and frees
tomorrow: what's the strangest thing a mother could sing to a baby?

lines: A KING AND A MERCHANT, BOTH BETRAYED.
cards: A friend drops you, and weeks later you're still checking what they post. In the Markandeya Purana, two men meet in a forest with that exact problem. King Suratha has lost his kingdom to enemies and to his own ministers.
The merchant Samadhi has been thrown out by his own wife and sons, for his money. Neither can stop worrying about the people who did it. Is my treasury safe?
Are my sons well? They know it makes no sense. So they ask the sage Medhas why.

teach.h: EVEN THE WISE ARE DRAWN IN.
teach.b: Medhas's answer opens the Devi Mahatmya, the glory of the Goddess, a long section set inside the Markandeya Purana.
Even the wise, he says, are drawn into clinging by the Goddess as Mahamaya, the great power that holds the world together, and when she's pleased, the same power sets a person free.
Then he tells them her stories: battles against demons the gods couldn't beat.

teach.h: A TEXT THAT LIVES IN THE EAR.
teach.b: This is a text that lives in the ear. Some families and temples recite it whole during Navaratri, the nine nights of the Goddess, and some keep the recording playing all through those mornings.
Its best-known hymn is built from one repeated shape.
To the goddess who lives in all beings as consciousness, and the line closes: namas tasyai, namas tasyai, namas tasyai, namo namah. Bow to her, bow to her, bow to her, again and again.
Then the same line again, with a new word: as sleep, as hunger, as patience, as mother.
And one surprise in the list: bhranti, error, confusion, the very thing troubling the two men. The refrain doesn't argue. It just keeps bowing.
At the end of the story, the king asks for his kingdom back, and the merchant asks for the knowledge that sets him free of mine.

how: During Navaratri some Hindu households and temples recite the Devi Mahatmya, also called the Durga Saptashati or Chandi Path, often over the nine nights; others play a recording of it in the mornings.

o: a song sung only at the end of Navaratri
a Purana told in the sage Markandeya's name
a sage's diary of his very long life

games.q: who's who in the forest — tap the pairs.
p: a king who lost his kingdom
a merchant thrown out by his family
the power that binds and frees

s: the Devi Mahatmya is a separate book with no Purana around it
it sits inside the Markandeya Purana, though it's often recited on its own.
Medhas says the men cling because they aren't wise
he says even the wise are drawn in by the Goddess as Mahamaya.
the hymn names the Goddess even as error and confusion
bhranti, error, is among the forms the refrain bows to.

games.q: a friend can't stop checking an ex's posts, knows it makes no sense, and feels stupid. what does the Devi Mahatmya's opening offer?
o: only the weak feel this; the wise never do.
even the wise are drawn in, and the same power that binds can set free.
cut off every feeling for people who hurt you.
games.why: Medhas tells the king and the merchant that clinging catches even the wise, through Mahamaya, who, when pleased, also frees.

practice: Find one steady sound near you: a fan, traffic, the hum of a fridge, your own breathing. Listen to it the way someone listens to a long recitation, not to understand it, just to stay with it.
When your mind slides off toward someone you're worried about, notice, and come back to the sound.

wordCard.voice: The Markandeya. The Purana that holds the Devi Mahatmya, which opens with two men who can't stop caring.

orig.note: Sanskrit: the great power (maha, great; maya) by which the Goddess holds the world, binding and freeing.

carryVoice: Hold onto this: Mahamaya, the Goddess's power. What binds you is also what sets you free. More tomorrow.
